notes.b: Fish spoils quickly, so you judge it by sight, touch and smell, and by how reliable the seller is. A good buyer checks each sign in turn, because a fish that fails on one is usually failing on others.
points: Eyes should be bright, clear and bulging (plump); sunken, cloudy or dull eyes show the fish is old.
Gills should be bright red; grey or brown gills show the fish is not fresh.
Flesh should be firm and elastic, springing back when pressed; soft flesh that keeps the dent is stale.
Skin and scales should be moist and shiny, with tight, unbroken scales and no bruising or breaks in the skin.
Smell should be mild and fresh, like the sea; a strong or unpleasant smell means the fish is spoiling.
Shellfish should be alive and heavy for their size. Mussels should be closed, because an open mussel that does not close when tapped is dead and is discarded.
Smoked fish should look glossy; frozen fish should be solid with its packaging intact and no signs of thawing or freezer burn; canned fish should be in an undamaged, undented can within its date.

Buy from a reliable, hygienic retailer where the fish is displayed on ice or refrigerated, check the date on packaged fish, and buy fish in season, when it is better and cheaper. Medium-size fish have the best flavour.
Get the fish home quickly, using a cool bag or ice, and refrigerate it straight away so it does not warm up on the way.
notes.tip: Guidelines for buying fresh fish is a long-answer question. Give eyes, gills, flesh, skin and scales, and smell, then shellfish closed and alive, then a reliable hygienic source, ice, the date and in season. Where fish products are asked for, add smoked fish glossy and frozen fish solid. For mussels, use the tap test: do not say every open mussel is dead.

notes.h: Who checks fish safety in Ireland
notes.b: Buyers also rely on official checks on the fish they buy. This is background, not a buying guideline.
points: The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (set up in 2007 under the Sea-Fisheries and Maritime Jurisdiction Act 2006) carries out official controls on fish and shellfish from production to distribution, under a service contract with the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI).

notes.b: Fish spoils faster than meat, so it must be used or processed as soon as possible after it is caught. Its flesh is soft, high in water and has little connective tissue, and its fat and enzymes act quickly. There are three main causes.
points: Oxidative rancidity: the fats in the fish, especially the polyunsaturated fat of oily fish, react with oxygen in the air, giving an unpleasant smell and taste.
Bacterial action starts before death: a fish caught in a net struggles and uses up its glycogen stores (the sugar store in the flesh).
When glycogen is present, it converts to lactic acid, which is a preservative. If lactic acid is not present, the fish goes off quickly.
Bacteria work on the flesh and produce trimethylamine, a strong-smelling nitrogen compound, which is what gives spoiled fish its smell.
Enzymic activity: enzymes in the flesh cause deterioration even at low temperatures, so spoilage continues, slowly, even in the fridge.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to outline the main causes of spoilage, or to explain two factors. Name oxidative rancidity, bacterial action with glycogen, lactic acid and trimethylamine, and enzymes. Do not say lactic acid causes spoilage: a struggling fish has little glycogen, so little lactic acid forms and bacteria spread faster. Trimethylamine is made by bacteria and gives the strong smell.

notes.b: Storage cannot stop spoilage, only slow it, so fresh fish keeps for a short time only. Good storage keeps it cold and keeps it from contaminating other food.
points: Chilling slows bacterial growth and enzyme action but does not stop them, so fresh fish is kept chilled, below 5 °C, packed on crushed ice until it is used.
Raw fish is stored on the lowest shelf of the fridge in a covered container, so that drips cannot contaminate other food.
Raw fish is kept apart from cooked and ready-to-eat foods to prevent cross-contamination.
Covering the fish stops it drying out and stops its smell passing to other food.
Fresh fish is used on the day of purchase or as soon as possible after it.
Oily fish deteriorates faster than white fish because its fat goes rancid; this also limits how long it keeps frozen.
notes.tip: For storing fresh fish at home, give: below 5 °C, covered, lowest shelf, away from cooked food, and use quickly.

notes.b: Freezing is the best way to keep fish for longer. At freezer temperature the water in the flesh is held as ice, so micro-organisms cannot grow and enzyme action is inactivated. It slows or stops spoilage but does not kill all bacteria, which can grow again after thawing.
points: Freeze only fish that is very fresh and of best quality; freezing cannot improve fish that is already poor in quality.
Turn the freezer to its fast-freeze setting 3 to 4 hours before freezing the fish, so the fish freezes quickly.
Freeze fish in usable quantities, so that only the amount needed is thawed.
Do not freeze more than about a tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24 hours, so that the food already frozen stays frozen.
Wrap fish tightly in moisture-proof packaging or vacuum pack it, to prevent freezer burn (dried-out patches) and oxidation, because air in the packaging lets oily fish go rancid.
Label each package with the name of the fish and the date, so you can use it within the time on the pack.
Store frozen fish at −18 °C or below.
Thaw frozen fish slowly in the fridge and do not refreeze it once thawed raw.
notes.tip: For the general rules for freezing food, give fast-freeze, one tenth of capacity, best quality, usable quantities, packaging and labelling. Do not say freezing kills micro-organisms or sterilises the fish: it stops them multiplying.

notes.h: Effects of freezing and its advantages and disadvantages
notes.b: Freezing changes fish very little, which is why it is so widely used, but it has costs too.
points: Colour and flavour are largely unchanged and nutrients are well kept.
Texture may change, and some B vitamins and extractives (flavour compounds) are lost on thawing.
Poor wrapping causes freezer burn, and air in the packaging lets oily fish go rancid.
Advantages: freezing is simple and safe, loses little nutrient, and allows bulk buying and out-of-season fish.
Disadvantages: it needs packaging and freezer running costs.
notes.tip: If asked for an advantage and a disadvantage of freezing fish, pair one from each list, for example little nutrient loss against the cost of packaging and running the freezer.

keyTerms.definition: The deterioration of fish fats when they react with oxygen in the air, producing an unpleasant smell and taste.
A strong-smelling nitrogen compound produced by bacteria acting on fish flesh, which gives spoiled fish its odour.
A stored carbohydrate in fish muscle that normally converts to lactic acid after death, helping to preserve the flesh.
A preservative acid formed from glycogen in the flesh of freshly caught fish.
The action of enzymes in the flesh that breaks down the fish and causes deterioration, even at low temperatures.
Freezing food quickly at a very low temperature so that small ice crystals form and the food keeps its quality.
Drying and discolouration of the surface of frozen food caused by poor packaging that lets in air.
The transfer of bacteria from raw food to cooked or ready-to-eat food.

factCards.term: Five signs of fresh whole fish
factCards.definition: Bright, bulging eyes; bright red gills; firm, elastic flesh; moist, shiny skin with tight scales; and a mild sea smell.
Oxidative rancidity, bacterial action and enzymic activity.

factCards.term: Four rules for freezing fresh fish
factCards.definition: Freeze only very fresh fish; use the fast-freeze setting beforehand; freeze in usable quantities; and label with name and date.

factCards.term: Two effects of freezing on the quality of fish
factCards.definition: Texture may change as ice crystals form, and some B vitamins may be lost.

factCards.term: Two checks on shellfish when buying
factCards.definition: Shellfish should be alive, and mussels should be closed.

questions.prompt: Outline four guidelines to follow when buying fresh fish.
questions.model: Any four of: eyes bright and bulging; gills bright red; flesh firm and springing back when pressed; skin moist and shiny with tight scales and no bruising; mild sea smell; shellfish heavy for its size and alive, with mussels closed; buy from a reliable hygienic retailer where the fish is kept on ice; check the sell-by date; buy fish in season.

questions.prompt: Explain three causes of fish spoilage and describe how freezing fresh fish, when carried out correctly, slows or stops that spoilage.
questions.model: Oxidative rancidity: fish fats react with oxygen in the air, causing an unpleasant smell and taste; oily fish is especially affected. Bacterial action: after death the fish has used up its glycogen, so lactic acid is not formed to preserve it; bacteria then work on the flesh and produce trimethylamine, a strong-smelling compound. Enzymic activity: enzymes in the flesh cause deterioration even at low temperatures. Freezing: the fish must be very fresh and frozen quickly, using the fast-freeze setting, so that small ice crystals form. Freezing at a low temperature, held at −18 °C or below, stops microbial growth and inactivates enzymes, as the water is held as ice. Wrapping in moisture-proof packaging or vacuum packing prevents freezer burn and reduces oxidation. The fish should be labelled with name and date, and thawed in the fridge without being refrozen.
